head: Bush stone-curlews have hatched chicks on Phillip Island for the first time in 50 years.
summary: Wild bush stone-curlew chicks have hatched on Phillip Island, off the Victorian coast, for the first time in more than half a century. Phillip Island Nature Parks has released over 70 of the birds since 2024 alongside the Australian National University, the Odonata Foundation and the Penguin Foundation, and added 12 more on November 4 drawn from five wildlife sanctuaries around the country. Paula Wasiak of ANU calls the hatching a milestone for the programme, and Duncan Sutherland, who runs it for the Nature Parks, says the point now is a population genetically diverse and sturdy enough to carry on by itself.

place: Llanos de Challe National Park, Atacama, Chile
head: More than 200 kinds of flower have come up at once in the Atacama.
summary: The driest desert on Earth is in colour again around Llanos de Challe National Park in northern Chile, where more than 200 plant species are flowering after winter rain of over 150 millimetres in places, the heaviest since 1997. Moisés Grimberg, who administers the park, describes the ground as a seed bank that only needs water, and botanists from Chile's national seed bank are out collecting specimens from patches no one has recorded in flower before. The park usually takes about 10,000 visitors a year and has had 15,000 in a few weeks; by the middle of this month the flowers will dry, drop their seed back into the sand and wait for the next rain.

head: A Balinese farmer is breeding fireflies back into the fields he grew up beside.
summary: Wayan Wardika watched fireflies over his village's rice fields as a boy and then watched them go, thinned out by lighting, pesticides and building; since founding Bring Back the Light in 2020 he has released close to 20,000 larvae and adults, and the counts around Taro are climbing again. Lead scientist Cindy Chayani's team raises the larvae in purpose-built terrariums for up to two years and lets about 90 percent of the adults go, while Wardika composts manure from a facility that keeps Bali's sacred white cattle and brews a pesticide from fermented market waste. Breeding alone will not hold them, so he is trying to move 35 neighbouring farmers off agricultural chemicals — four so far, each given free compost and paid back for what the changeover costs them — because, as he puts it, if we don't see fireflies, there is something wrong with the ecosystem.

head: Loggerhead turtles keep nesting further west, and Italy's beach clubs are learning to share the sand.
summary: Loggerheads that for decades nested almost only in Greece, Türkiye and Cyprus now come ashore along Italy, France and Spain, where the first confirmed Spanish nest was found in 2001 and nesting has been annual since 2014. Sandra Hochscheid of the Stazione Zoologica Anton Dohrn follows nesting females by satellite, and Carlos Carreras at the University of Barcelona has traced the newcomers' genomes back to eastern Mediterranean and Caribbean populations; a study in Campania found 87 percent of nests in 2022 and 2023 lay within reach of beachfront lighting, and 82 percent needed someone to step in so the hatchlings went seaward rather than inland. Owners of the lidi who once brushed the tracks away now telephone them in, and Ascea, which has already dimmed its promenade, will require low-impact lighting on every beach concession from 2027.

head: Horseshoe crabs have been confirmed in a second Philippine province.
summary: Researchers interviewed 142 residents across four municipalities of Tawi-Tawi and logged sightings in Bongao, Simunul, Sitangkai and Panglima Sugala, the first record of the animals anywhere in the Philippines outside Palawan. Ivane Pedrosa-Gerasmio of Mindanao State University–Iligan Institute of Technology first heard of them at a Bongao market in December 2023; residents call them bangkas, after the shape of a boat, and the two kinds described resemble the endangered tri-spine and the mangrove horseshoe crab. More than half of those interviewed believe numbers are falling, and her student Quesie Tolero Omnos argues the new record should guide what local councils choose to protect.

head: Shearwaters flying home through the night drift off course, the way we get jet lag.
summary: Twenty years of GPS tracks from 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters — 3,688 trips in all, 1,837 of them homeward across the Irish Sea and the northeast Atlantic — show the birds veering clockwise by as much as 15 degrees when they fly in the dark. Patrick Lewin, an ecologist at the University of Oxford, and his colleagues report in Science that the drift looks like an internal clock briefly out of step with the sun, the same mismatch that leaves a long-haul passenger groggy. It costs the birds very little: on a homeward leg of roughly 1,000 kilometres, a seven-degree error adds about five.

head: A second tiger is loose in the Ili delta, where none has lived for 70 years.
summary: Kazakhstan's ecology ministry let a male Amur tiger, named Amur, out into the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve on October 31, three months after a female called Umit walked out of her enclosure on July 31. Both wear satellite collars; they came from a group of four tigers brought from Russia's Khabarovsk Territory in May, and the reserve has been laying in their food first — 30 kulans were moved across from Altyn-Emel national park in September, along with Bukhara deer. Two cubs are still under supervision and will go out when keepers judge them ready; the aim, set with the Amur Tiger Centre and WWF, is a population in the Ili delta and southern Balkhash that breeds without help.

head: Beavers are going back into the waters around Loch Ness after 500 years.
summary: NatureScot approved a licence on October 30 for Trees for Life and the Beaver Trust to release up to 15 beaver families into the River Ness catchment over three years, five centuries after the last beaver was recorded at the loch. The animals will come from farmland elsewhere in Scotland where they are damaging prime agricultural ground, be trapped under licence and health-screened before being moved; more than 73 percent of those who answered NatureScot's consultation supported the plan, and the agency says it is taking seriously the concerns raised by land managers, fisheries managers and people living in the catchment. The first releases could come within weeks, in a catchment NatureScot identified back in 2022 as one of the most suitable in Scotland.

head: Mexican biologists are growing mangroves on mounds borrowed from Aztec farmers.
summary: In the Alvarado Lagoons of Veracruz, the Mexican nonprofit REVIVE plants mangrove seedlings on chinampas — raised mounds of earth of the kind Aztec farmers built — so that young trees sit above water that would otherwise drown them. The biologist Aníbal Ramírez Soto turned to the method in 2006 after a first attempt at planting in rows failed; about 2,000 trees went into the first few hundred mounds, more than 4,000 more arrived on their own with the tides, and by year eight the canopy had closed over 80 percent of the site. The project now runs to some 15,000 mounds across 40 hectares, and the team has released about 80 Morelet's crocodiles in the belief that they keep channels open and shift sediment, an effect crocodile specialists call plausible but not yet demonstrated.

head: Fishers on Pemba Island asked for marine reserves, and got 1,300 square kilometres.
summary: Tanzania has gazetted the North-East and South-East Pemba conservation areas, about 1,300 square kilometres of reef, seagrass and fishing ground off Zanzibar's second island. The request came from fishers in Tumbe and more than twenty other villages who had watched their catches thin, and who then worked with the Department of Blue Economy and Fisheries, the Wildlife Conservation Society, Blue Alliance and Mwambao to write no-take zones, spawning closures and gear rules into village by-laws. Blue Alliance reports patrols up by more than half and illegal fishing down about 45 percent, and the next task is building income that does not depend on the net — sea cucumber farming, seaweed drying, tourism.

head: Tigers, leopards, and elephant herds return to a restored Assam grassland.
summary: In Assam's Sonitpur district, the Sonai Rupai Wildlife Sanctuary has documented tigers, leopards, and large elephant herds returning to roughly 300 hectares of grassland restored over the past year and a half. The Western Assam Wildlife Division reclaimed the land after the Indian Army handed back a former camp, desilted about 100,000 cubic meters of wetland, and widened patrol routes, with the Wildlife Institute of India confirming two resident tigers through camera-trap surveys. Divisional Forest Officer Piraisoodan B says the department is clearing the sanctuary's remaining encroachment in phases, giving each reclaimed patch time to recover before the next begins.

head: Pakistan joined its Indus river dolphin sanctuaries into one 400-kilometre protected corridor.
summary: The Punjnad Indus River Dolphin Sanctuary, created in June 2026, protects nearly 200 kilometres of river in Punjab and connects with existing reserves in Sindh. A 2025 study estimated 1,987 dolphins, up from 617 in 2001, with 99 percent living in a 690-kilometre stretch between the Chashma and Sukkur barrages. Gillnets caused 52 percent of documented deaths from 2008 to 2023, and they remain the main threat the new protections must address.

head: Asháninka fire brigades brought wildfires in 45 Peruvian communities down to zero.
summary: Across 45 Asháninka communities in Peru's Ene River region, wildfires fell from 25 in 2023 to nine in 2024, and none were recorded in 2025. Community members trained as certified firefighters watch for smoke by satellite, drone and radio under the Paamari programme, run by the Central Asháninka of the Ene River with the charity Cool Earth. Burned area dropped from 2,648 hectares to 492 in a year when fires across Peru destroyed 63,000 hectares.

head: A bird unseen for thirteen years reappeared in an Ivorian rainforest.
summary: Field researchers photographed a Ghana cuckooshrike in Côte d'Ivoire's Taï National Park in June, the species' first confirmed sighting since 2013. Stephanie Bartlett and Paulo Ditzel of the International Bird Conservation Partnership spent six months surveying West Africa's forests before capturing what may be the best photographs ever taken of the bird. The team plans to return to Taï within the year to survey further and strengthen ties with the local researchers protecting the park's shrinking forest.

head: Pakistan linked two river reserves into a single 400-kilometer sanctuary for the world's rarest dolphin.
summary: The government's new Punjnad Indus River Dolphin Sanctuary now connects with an existing reserve in Sindh, giving the critically endangered, functionally blind species a continuous protected corridor along the river. A 2025 survey counted roughly 1,987 of the dolphins, up from a low of 617 in 2001, though gillnets still cause more than half of recorded deaths. WWF-Pakistan biologist Uzma Khan says the connected corridor lets dolphins move between feeding grounds without crossing the busiest fishing waters.

head: Genetic testing revealed a fourth gentoo penguin species hiding on a remote sub-Antarctic island.
summary: An international team analyzing genomes, body size, calls, and breeding schedules confirmed that gentoo penguins on France's remote Kerguelen Islands form their own species, Pygoscelis kerguelensis — the first new penguin species named in more than a century. The researchers, publishing in Communications Biology, found that three populations long treated as mere subspecies are genetically distinct enough to split the familiar gentoo penguin into four separate species. Conservationists say the finer-grained map gives each population, several already vulnerable to warming seas, a clearer claim to its own protection.

head: A tropical heat pool sent 695 billion tons of extra snow onto East Antarctica.
summary: Between 2021 and 2023, satellites recorded East Antarctica's largest ice-mass gain on record, equal to about four years of the continent's average annual loss. Researcher Qinghua Ding traced the cause to unusual warming in the tropical Pacific-Indian "warm pool," which sent an atmospheric river of moisture toward Queen Mary Land and Wilkes Land as heavy snow. Only 9 percent of the anomaly was linked to human-caused warming, and researchers say the gain is temporary, not a reversal of the ice sheet's long-term decline.

head: Wildlife officers built a fifty-foot tunnel so rare possums could find mates across a highway.
summary: Victoria's Great Alpine Road cuts straight through the range of the mountain pygmy-possum at Little Mount Higginbotham, splitting a population of roughly 150 four-inch marsupials from mates on the other side. The Department of Environment, Land, Water and Planning built a nearly 50-foot underpass beneath the road, and over two summers 30 possums used it, crossing in about 15 seconds each, while Zoos Victoria's Healesville Sanctuary tracked hibernation by thermal camera. Fewer than 2,000 of the possums are left in the wild, and the sanctuary recorded 12 joeys born this past March — a sign the tunnel is doing its job.

head: Six Irrawaddy dolphin calves were born in the Mekong this year.
summary: Five calves surfaced in Cambodia's Kratie province and one in neighboring Stung Treng, lifting the river's known population of the endangered dolphins to about 118. Seventy-two river guards now patrol 180 kilometers of protected habitat, working with WWF-Cambodia to curb the illegal gillnets and electrofishing that helped cut the population from roughly 200 in the late 1990s. The dolphins have already vanished from the Mekong Delta and Tonle Sap Lake, so each calf gives the fishing communities whose tourism depends on them one more reason to keep the patrols funded.

head: Two reintroduced beavers raised a Cheshire peatland's groundwater nearly forty-fold.
summary: Ecologist Melanie Baker's four-year study found that two Eurasian beavers, released into a fenced 4.5-hectare enclosure at Hatch Mere in Cheshire, raised local groundwater levels by up to 37 times and lifted surface water by a median of 50 centimeters. Working with the Cheshire Wildlife Trust, the beavers built dams that kept the peatland measurably wetter through the dry summer of 2022 than the surrounding land. Baker says the findings point to beavers as a low-cost way to make Britain's drained peat bogs more resilient to drought.

head: A giant anteater turned up in an Argentine reserve that hadn't seen one in forty years.
summary: A male giant anteater was spotted last year at the Alma Guaraní Natural Reserve in Argentina's Corrientes province, the region's first recorded sighting of the species since 1986. Researcher Rosario Montiel of the National University of the Northeast called the appearance "the first register of the giant anteater in 40 years in Corrientes province, and it was spontaneous," arriving after four years of restoration work returned ecological function to more than 150 of the reserve's 6,400 hectares, with native trees replanted on eleven more. Montiel's team now hopes to bring in female anteaters to keep the newcomer company, though roaming dogs and fragmented farmland still make it hard for the animals to move between forest patches.
